verses.translation_literal: Of David. To you, YHWH, I call, my rock; do not be deaf from me, lest you be silent from me and I be made equal with those who go down to the pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. To you I call, LORD. You, my rock, my only footing. Do not turn a deaf ear. Do not go quiet on me. For if you are silent, I am no better than those who go down to the pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a prayer from a man at the edge, and the whole psalm turns on one fear: that the heavens answer with nothing. The verb pair matters. 'Be deaf' (תחרש) and 'be silent' (תחשה) are two different roots, and the Hebrew puts them side by side to name a God who either does not hear or does not speak. The KJV, YLT and Webster flatten both to 'silent'; the ASV keeps 'deaf'. Meiri notes that the sense is to make oneself deaf, to act as if one hears nothing. Actors should not play it as a polite request. 'Rock' (צור) is the language of a cliff or a fortress, a physical refuge, and it is the first thing the speaker calls God before he begs.

The 'pit' (בור) is the grave, or Sheol, the cistern-like hole of the dead where there is no praise. 'Go down' is the standard verb for dying, and Radak reads it as the fate of the wicked. For an ancient Israelite, the terror is not only death but being counted among those whom God no longer answers. The KJV 'I become like them' is fair, but the Hebrew is stronger: 'I will be made equal with', as if weighed on the same scale. Note that the Hebrew verse includes 'Of David', which the KJV numbers as a separate verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Be deaf', or 'make yourself deaf'. It is a different root from תחשה in the same line. Meiri argues that it means to act as if one does not hear, not merely to be silent.
'Be silent', 'hold your peace'. Radak connects it to Ecclesiastes 3:7, 'a time to be silent'.
'Those who go down to the pit': the dead. The pit is both the grave and the underworld.

verses.translation_literal: Hear the sound of my supplications, in my crying for help to you, in my lifting my hands to the innermost room of your holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear the sound of my pleading. Hear me as I cry out to you, as I lift my hands toward the innermost room of your holy house.
verses.directors_commentary:
The body prays here. Lifted, open hands were the ordinary posture of petition in the ancient Near East, the palms spread toward the god as a beggar's hands are spread. Radak ties it to Solomon's prayer, 'his hands spread toward heaven' (1 Kings 8:54). The speaker is not in the sanctuary, only turned toward it.

The KJV 'holy oracle' is a Latin leftover. The Hebrew דביר is the back chamber of the sanctuary, the room behind the curtain where the ark stood, the place only the high priest entered, once a year (Leviticus 16). Metzudat Zion defines it simply as the house of the holy of holies. Praying toward it is praying toward the place where God's presence is said to dwell, and Radak also allows that the phrase may mean heaven itself. Two verbs of voice are paired: 'supplications' (תחנונים, a plea for grace) and 'cry for help' (שוע), the cry of someone who needs rescue now.

philological_notes.note: The innermost room of the temple, the Holy of Holies. Metzudat Zion identifies it as the house of the holy of holies. Radak adds that it may stand for heaven.
A plea for favour, from the root 'to be gracious'; it asks for mercy, not for justice.

verses.translation_literal: Do not drag me with the wicked, and with the doers of wickedness, speakers of peace with their neighbours, and evil in their heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not drag me off with the wicked. Not with those who do harm, whose mouths say peace to their neighbours while evil sits in their hearts.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb משך is physical: to pull or drag, as one drags an animal or a net. The plea is not 'do not let me sin' but 'do not haul me away with them' to their fate. Radak reads it as dragging towards the death of the wicked (and compares Job 21:33); Malbim hears a net. KJV 'draw me not away' softens a rough word into something genteel.

The heart of the verse is the contrast of mouth and heart: 'speakers of peace' (shalom!) with 'evil in their heart'. In a village society, greeting your neighbour with shalom is the basic act of trust; the men described use it as cover. Radak notes that the wicked rarely show themselves. Malbim sees the danger as precisely this: the speaker cannot guard against them because they look friendly. KJV 'mischief' is too small for רעה, which is plain 'evil' or 'harm'. The Hebrew also has no relative 'which' as the KJV adds; the participles simply stand in apposition.

philological_notes.note: 'Drag, draw, pull', as with a rope or a net. Radak takes it as being pulled toward death with the wicked.
'Doers of wickedness', a stock phrase for those who work harm. The root פעל, 'to do', is echoed in verse 4 and again, as God's deeds, in verse 5.
'Speakers of peace': the greeting or promise of well-being used to hide hostile intent.

verses.translation_literal: Give to them according to their work, and according to the evil of their deeds; according to the work of their hands give to them; return their recompense to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give them what their work has earned. Give them the measure of their evil. As their hands have worked, so give to them. Let their own deed come back upon them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hardest verse in the psalm for a modern ear, and it should be played without apology and without relish. The speaker asks not for something new but for symmetry: the same hands, the same work, handed back. The verse is built as a hammer of repeated words: 'give' (תן) twice, 'work' (פעל, מעשה) three times, 'hands', and finally 'return' (השב). The KJV smooths this into 'desert' and 'endeavours', losing the sense of boomerang. The Hebrew גמול is a recompense, and the verb 'return' says it is something that was theirs to begin with.

In a world without police, prayer is the appeal court. Radak says God alone knows their hearts, so judgment is left with God, a point that links to verse 3: the people the speaker cannot detect are the ones he hands to the one who can. Malbim reads the justice as measure for measure, so that those who spoke one thing and hid another will themselves be misled. Every command is second person singular, addressed to God.

philological_notes.note: 'Deeds, doings', always used of conduct, and usually bad conduct, in the Hebrew Bible. The KJV 'endeavours' is too neutral.
'Recompense': what is paid back for what was done. The verb השב 'return' makes it a repayment.

verses.translation_literal: For they do not discern the deeds of YHWH, and the work of his hands; he will tear them down and not build them.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they will not see what the LORD has done. They do not look at the work of his hands. So he will pull them down, and he will not raise them up again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the judgment is a failure to look. 'Discern' (בין) means to attend closely, to understand, and the wicked will not do it. Ibn Ezra says that if they understood the LORD's deeds they would not do wickedness, for they would know he overthrows them. Radak takes the deeds of the LORD as the natural order, heaven and earth, from which one learns the power of the maker.

The wordplay reaches back: in verse 4 the wicked had 'work' and 'hands'; here those words return for God ('the work of his hands'). Their work against his work. The answer is a builder's pair of verbs, 'tear down' (הרס) and 'build' (בנה). The KJV 'destroy' and 'build up' keep the picture, but 'regard not' is vague, and 'operation' is archaic. Whether it is a prediction or still prayer is disputed: Ibn Ezra and Radak allow that the verbs are a wish, and Meiri reads it as a prayer for permanent ruin. The Hebrew has the plain imperfect, so play it as certainty.

philological_notes.note: 'Discern, give attention to'. The failure is of perception more than of knowledge, and the sin lies in not looking.
'Tear down and not build': the builder's reversal of the work. Radak links 'tear down' to their 'deeds' as a mirrored answer.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed be YHWH, for he has heard the sound of my supplications.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD! He has heard. He has heard the sound of my pleading.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes in one breath. The silence feared in verse 1 is gone, and the same phrase that opened the plea, 'the sound of my supplications' (verse 2), returns as an answered one. Nothing in the text says how the answer came. Ibn Ezra and Meiri call it prophetic certainty, thanks given as if the answer had already arrived; Radak links it to David's later danger (2 Samuel 21:16-17). Read it as relief, not as a cheerful sermon.

The KJV 'he hath heard' is correct, but it loses the echo: the first-person plea was 'hear' (שמע), and the thanks is 'he has heard' (שמע), the same root. The prayer is closed by its own word.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle, 'blessed', a statement or acclamation and not a command: 'Blessed is YHWH'.
The perfect 'he has heard' answers the imperative 'hear' of verse 2. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as the certainty of prophecy.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH is my strength and my shield; in him my heart has trusted, and I was helped, and my heart exulted, and from my song I will give thanks to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is my strength, the LORD my shield. In him my heart trusted, and I was helped. So my heart leaps. And out of my own song I will thank him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm has now moved from fear to a song, and the verse should be sung or nearly so. Two military images open it: 'strength' (עז) and 'shield' (מגן). The shield was the small round or the large body shield of a soldier; for a king like David, God is the one who stands in front. BBE's 'breastplate' is not the ordinary sense of מגן. Radak, reading the psalm against David's wars, says the 'shield' saved him from the men who tried to strike him.

The verbs run in sequence: trusted, was helped, exulted, will thank. The KJV adds 'therefore', which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew simply lines up the events, and the joy follows the help without being argued from it. 'Heart' (לב) appears twice, and the Hebrew sense of 'heart' is the mind and will, not only feeling, as Radak says when he reads 'heart' as the intellect. The last clause, 'from my song', means that the thanks will be made of the speaker's own songs, a point on which Radak and Metzudat David agree.

philological_notes.note: 'My strength'. Radak reads the ayin with a shureq (עוזי). An editor's note in the printed Radak adds that other exact copies have a qubbutz under the ayin and a dagesh in the zayin (עֻזִּי): the same u-vowel, written in two ways, so the sense does not change.
'Exult, leap for joy'; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'rejoice'. It is a stronger word than KJV 'rejoiceth' suggests.
'And from my song': the thanks is drawn out of his own songs, per Radak; Metzudat David reads it as 'I will thank him with one of the songs I have said'.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to him

verses.translation_literal: YHWH is strength to them, and he is a refuge of the salvations of his anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is strength to his people. He is the stronghold where his anointed one finds rescue.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'I' of the psalm opens into a 'them'. The Hebrew למו is an old poetic form of 'to them', and the plural is the point: the speaker's own strength (verse 7) is also the strength of a whole people. The KJV 'their strength' keeps it, but the reader is left to guess who 'they' are. Radak and Malbim read Israel, the people for whom David prays; the Targum keeps the plain 'to them' (להון) without naming anyone; Ibn Ezra reads it as those who help. Play it as a quiet widening of the circle, from a lone man to a nation, before the final prayer.

The 'anointed' (משיח) is a king, set apart by oil, and in the Hebrew text the word is singular, 'his anointed'. BBE 'king' is an interpretation. Radak says David says it of himself, as he does in 2 Samuel 23:1. KJV 'saving strength' hides that the Hebrew is a plural abstract, 'salvations' (ישועות): a place of repeated rescues. מעוז is a fortress or refuge, the high wall behind which a besieged people lives.

philological_notes.note: A poetic form of 'to them', plural. Ibn Ezra rejects a reading of it as 'to him' and takes it as the people and the helpers.
'Refuge of salvations': a fortress where rescue is found. The plural of ישועה suggests repeated or complete deliverance.
'His anointed', one set apart by oil. Radak identifies him with David, who uses the word of himself.

verses.translation_literal: Save your people, and bless your inheritance, and shepherd them, and carry them until the age.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save your people. Bless the ones who are your own. Be their shepherd, and carry them, now and for all time.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on four commands, short and rhythmic, and the last two are shepherd's work. 'Shepherd' (רעה) is the word of the pasture, to lead to grass and water; KJV 'feed' is too narrow, but it follows Rashi and Metzudat David, who read it as 'pasture'. Radak compares Isaiah 40:11, 'like a shepherd he feeds his flock'. 'Carry' (נשא) is the shepherd lifting the weak lamb on his shoulder; the KJV 'lift them up' leaves out the carrying. Ibn Ezra also hears the sense of setting them high, out of the reach of beasts.

'Inheritance' (נחלה) is land held as a family's permanent share. To call the people God's 'inheritance' is to say they are his own plot, not to be sold. The last phrase, 'until the age' (עד העולם), has no end point: Radak reads it as for all time, and as the prayer that continues even after the speaker's death. The KJV 'for ever' is right. Note the full circle: the psalm began with one man's cry to a silent God and ends with a whole people carried by a shepherd.

philological_notes.note: 'Shepherd them': lead and feed as a shepherd. Rashi glosses it as pasture; Radak compares Isaiah 40:11. Not to be confused with 'evil' (רעה) of verse 3, which is spelled the same in the consonants but is a different root.
'And carry them' or 'lift them up'. Ibn Ezra reads it as placing them on a height beyond the reach of wild animals.
'Your inheritance': land or people held by hereditary right, never to be alienated. Metzudat David: Israel, whom God took as his inheritance.
